# Épi: Towards a Persistent, Self-Improving Agent for Autonomous Research

**Yue Huang**<sup>1,2</sup> **Zhangchen Xu**<sup>1,3</sup> **Xiaonan Luo**<sup>1,2</sup> **Zheyuan Liu**<sup>1,2</sup> **Lichi Li**<sup>1</sup>

**Yiping Wang**<sup>3</sup> **Peiyang Song**<sup>7</sup> **Eric Gabriel Ramos**<sup>4</sup> **Enze Xie**<sup>6</sup> **Olexandr Isayev**<sup>7</sup>

**Paul Liang**<sup>8</sup> **Nouha Dziri**<sup>9</sup> **Huan Sun**<sup>10</sup> **Jianfeng Gao**<sup>11</sup> **Ying Liu**<sup>5</sup> **Misha Sra**<sup>12</sup>

**Xiangliang Zhang**<sup>2</sup> **Alex Pentland**<sup>8,13</sup> **Zichen Chen**<sup>1,12,13</sup>

**Abstract**

We present Épi, an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and evolves its methods through accumulated experience. Épi combines persistent research history, hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to maintain research continuity, learn from experiments, and explore and revisit alternative approaches. Its experiments run across session boundaries, and a fixed verifier evaluates their outputs. Épi produced 120 record-setting results, comprising 20 numerical bound records across 12 families and 100 construction records across eight families. These include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the _n_-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact dual certificates establish that the Cohn–Elkies linear-programming bound cannot be sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Beyond numerical improvements, Épi gives a computer-assisted proof of Tuza’s conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We extend this research process to algorithmic coding with Épi-turbo, a lightweight configuration that develops executable solvers for tasks including vehicle routing, scheduling and production planning. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, Épi-turbo achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than x at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort. Épi is designed to support human understanding by connecting computational results to explicit methods and mathematical arguments that researchers can examine and build upon.

### 1 Introduction

Autonomous research agents must conduct experiments, interpret results and revise their methods over many interactions. FunSearch and AlphaEvolve demonstrate how agents can combine code generation with executable evaluation to discover new programs and constructions (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025). The AI Scientist-v2 extends automation to an experimental workflow (Yamada et al., 2025). When an investigation requires more work than one model session can support, however, the agent must manage three additional challenges.

**First, maintaining research continuity. Experiments and research decisions span multiple model sessions.** To continue an investigation, the agent needs access to running jobs, code, intermediate results and reasons for earlier decisions. Kosmos maintains a shared research state, InternAgent-1.5 organizes long-horizon memory, and ScienceFlow archives recoverable execution states (Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026). These mechanisms preserve information across steps. As the history grows, the agent must also select what a bounded model context needs: the current experimental state, relevant lessons and reasons

an earlier approach failed. This need motivates hierarchical memory that separates immediate context from reusable experience.

Second, learning from experimental experience. An agent needs to turn experimental observations into knowledge that guides subsequent decisions. This requires identifying which choices produced a result, under what conditions the method applies and which evidence supports the lesson. The agent must retain this knowledge and retrieve it for relevant tasks. MemoHarness addresses experience reuse by building a memory bank during training and retrieving execution diagnoses and reusable patterns to adapt the harness at test time (Huang et al., 2026). In an ongoing research investigation, the agent must also update its memory as new experiments arrive, linking each lesson to the conditions and evidence that support it.

Third, exploring alternatives and backtracking. A single research direction explores only part of the available methods. The AI Scientist-v2 uses agentic tree search to develop experimental alternatives, and ScienceFlow can resume from archived executable states (Yamada et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). These systems demonstrate the value of branching and backtracking. For research with checkable outputs, the agent must preserve each alternative’s implementation and evidence, compare candidates under a common evaluation rule and recover earlier work when new findings make it useful.

To address these challenges, we introduce Épi, a persistent and evolving autonomous research agent. Épi uses hierarchical memory to resume investigations and retrieve experience from earlier work. It maintains versioned branches to develop alternative methods and backtrack to saved implementations, and incorporates independent review when assessing evidence and choosing its next experiment. The agent operates in verifiable research environments that evolve between campaigns, where a campaign is a complete investigation that may span multiple model sessions. Within a campaign, every branch uses the same feasibility checks, objective and comparison value. A verified finding can then establish a new reference or motivate a new task for the next campaign. Persistent execution and storage carry the research state across sessions.

Mathematical discovery provides a concrete demonstration of this research process: the agent develops methods whose outputs can be checked as constructions, bounds or proofs. We also evaluate its applicability to algorithmic coding, where the agent must design and implement a solver that handles new problem instances efficiently. Our lightweight configuration, Épi-turbo, achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than x on 30 FrontierOR tasks at 64% of its model cost, using the same underlying model and reasoning effort (Section 6). These tasks include routing, scheduling, production planning and graph optimization.

Our contributions are an autonomous research agent that integrates hierarchical memory, branching and independent review to sustain and refine its investigations; a verification protocol that evaluates changing research methods under a fixed ruler and gain floor; and a collection of 120 record-setting results, comprising 100 improved constructions and 20 numerical bounds. Each record improves a documented literature or registry reference for the same problem and normalization; we count one final result per instance or parameter setting, as detailed in Section 4. These results include an approximately 84-fold narrower interval for the _n_-queens constant and a more than 3.6-million-fold narrower rigorous interval for the quartic Feigenbaum attractor dimension. Exact certificates establish that the Cohn–Elkies bound is not sharp in dimensions 10 and 11. Épi also proves Tuza’s conjecture for split graphs with an eight-vertex clique part and at most three triangle-active neighborhood types, with arbitrary multiplicities. We release the constructions and supporting certificates (Epi Team, 2026).

Our goal is to connect self-improvement with human understanding: researchers should be able to inspect how a method evolves, explain why a result holds, and use that knowledge to guide further work. Épi retains implementations, experimental artifacts, and research notes across branches and sessions, allowing researchers to inspect the development of a method and assess its supporting evidence. Its constructions, certificates, and mathematical arguments further connect computational outputs to findings that researchers can examine and build upon (Section 8).

## 2 Research Setting

### 2.1 Problems and Evidence

We study research tasks with a reference result, an explicit budget and outputs that can be checked. A curator supplies the question and source material; the agent chooses the methods and experiments. To compare the agent’s output with the reference, we specify an evaluation rule, called a _ruler_. The ruler defines the submission format, feasibility conditions, objective, normalization and comparison value.<sup>1</sup>

The agent submits the information required to check its claim. For a packing task, it supplies coordinates and orientations. For an optimization bound, it may supply a dual vector or another certificate. For a proof task, it supplies witnesses and an argument explaining why the checked objects establish the stated claim.

For a minimization problem, we write \(V(x)\in\{0,1\}\) for the verifier’s feasibility decision, _f(x_) for the objective and _b_ for the reference value. We define the improvement as \(\Delta(x)=b-f(x)\). We also specify a positive _gain floor_ \(\delta>0\), the smallest improvement that the task counts as meaningful.<sup>2</sup> Épi accepts an improvement when

\(V(x)=1,\Delta(x)\ge\delta.\) (1)

For maximization, we instead define \(\Delta(x)=f(x)-b\). The positive floor excludes ties and admits an improvement exactly equal to the threshold. If a task imposes no minimum gain (\(\delta=0\)), we instead require \(\Delta(x)>0\). We fix the feasibility tolerances and gain floor before the investigation. The verifier uses the tolerances to check constraints, while Épi uses the floor to decide whether the improvement counts. For a rigorous numerical bound, we additionally require exact arithmetic or outward rounding that controls the numerical error.

We establish a new record by verifying feasibility and improvement over the best established result for the same problem and normalization. Each final artifact retains its comparison value, source and any rounding convention. For a theorem, the proof connects the verified objects to the full stated claim.

### 2.2 Campaigns and Sessions

We call a complete investigation a _campaign_. A campaign may contain several agent sessions and concurrent experiments. Each session gives the agent a bounded context in which to inspect evidence, modify code and choose its next action. Épi stores the research state outside that context and keeps experiments running across session boundaries. A later session retrieves the saved state and resumes the investigation.

The curator may provide a published construction as the initial reference. The agent can consult the literature, implement alternative methods and select experiments within the campaign’s budget. We keep model weights fixed in the campaigns reported here. The agent adapts its methods through experimental feedback, retrieved memory and independent review.

## 3 The Épi Research Loop

Figure 1 shows Épi’s research loop. The agent conducts experiments in verifiable environments and improves its methods through branching, hierarchical memory and independent review. We describe the evolving environments and the mechanisms supporting the agent’s self-improvement below.

### 3.1 Evolving Research Environments

Comparing research methods requires a common objective and consistent validity checks. We establish these before search by checking that the scorer reproduces the reference result, testing input validation and fixing<tbc>

These choices determine whether two values measure the same quantity on valid objects. We introduce the ruler to make them explicit before search. <sup>2</sup>Counting every positive score change as progress can include differences due to reporting precision or routine post-processing. We derive the floor from the objective’s granularity and known transformations, and record its rationale with the task. the configuration, feasibility checks and gain criterion. The verifier then evaluates every branch under this shared rule. This gives Épi a consistent basis for comparing methods throughout the investigation.

We also specify the evidence needed for each type of claim. The verifier checks geometric constraints for a construction. For a rigorous bound, we require a certificate with exact arithmetic or controlled numerical error. For a computer-assisted theorem, we require both the finite checks and a mathematical reduction showing why those checks establish the full statement. The agent must develop this reduction or certificate when the task requires one.

Épi’s research environments evolve with verified findings. Improved results provide new reference values for subsequent investigations, while new research questions motivate changes to task formulations, representations and verification requirements. We incorporate these changes when defining the next campaign. For example, a numerical estimate can lead to a certification task whose environment includes certificate representations and rigorous error control. Each campaign uses a fixed evaluation rule to compare methods, and successive campaigns build on the verified findings of earlier work.

## 3.2 Self-improving Research Agents

Épi improves its research methods through accumulated experience. The agent develops and compares alternatives on versioned branches, retains and retrieves experience through hierarchical memory, and uses independent review to reassess its research decisions. Together, these mechanisms allow Épi to refine its approach across experiments and campaigns.

Branches and backtracking. A single approach restricts which formulations and search regions the agent explores. Épi maintains branches to develop alternatives while preserving each method’s code and evidence. Each branch stores an implementation, tests and notes in a versioned repository. The agent saves changes as commits and can create a new branch from an earlier commit. It compares the resulting experiments under the same ruler.

The agent backtracks by returning to a saved implementation and trying a different continuation. It can also revisit an existing branch and extend the work already recorded there. When the agent abandons a branch, it records the reason and retains the branch for later inspection. For a packing problem, the agent might refine

**Hierarchical memory.** Drawing on work on human and agent memory (Atkinson and Shiffrin, 1968; Packer et al., 2023; Park et al., 2023), Épi uses hierarchical memory to accumulate and reuse research experience. Short-term memory supports the current investigation, while long-term memory retains experience for subsequent research. As illustrated in Figure 1, memory records include research context, lessons that capture reusable findings, and dead ends that document unproductive approaches and why they were abandoned. The agent retrieves these records to guide its next experiment and updates them as new evidence becomes available.

Épi stores code, artifacts and detailed research notes in a persistent filesystem and keeps retrievable lessons and dead ends in a memory store outside the model context. At a session boundary, the agent records its findings and a handover note identifying the current state and next steps. A subsequent session receives relevant memory records and can open the referenced files as needed. This supplies a bounded working context without replaying the full history of earlier sessions.

**Independent review.** The agent that develops a method also chooses which evidence to examine, giving its assessment a limited perspective. Prior work on self-correction motivates adding feedback from outside the agent’s own reasoning process (Huang et al., 2024); research on reward hacking further motivates checking whether a score increase reflects the intended task (Denison et al., 2024). Épi combines a separate review of research progress with artifact verification under the fixed ruler.

Épi supplies a review model with the score trajectory, attempted approaches, retrieved findings, comparison baseline and resource use. The reviewer assesses what the evidence supports and whether the agent’s interpretation of progress is justified. Épi records this assessment for subsequent sessions, and the agent uses it when selecting further experiments or revisiting a branch. We use a different model for an independent review and record the reviewer’s identity. The reviewer evaluates the research direction; the isolated verifier checks the candidate’s validity and gain.

**Research transparency.** Épi records alternative implementations, their experimental outcomes, and the assessments used to guide subsequent work. These records allow researchers to compare branches, inspect the evidence associated with a methodological change, and revisit the implementation on which a conclusion depends. Lessons summarize reusable findings, while references to code and experimental artifacts let researchers examine the evidence behind those summaries.

**Execution support.** We use Breadboard as Épi’s execution infrastructure. Breadboard provides isolated experimental environments, supports long-running jobs across model sessions and stores research history, including code, branch states and experimental outputs. It also runs the fixed verifier and preserves the state needed to recover and continue an investigation. The agent uses these services to execute experiments, inspect results and resume its research across sessions.

## 4 Experimental Results

### 4.1 Setup and Counting

We ran Épi over a few days using OpenAI frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6-Astra). Computational budgets were set per problem. Published methods and constructions supplied starting points for several campaigns, including the packing case in Section 5.1. Each comparison uses the same task and evaluation convention for the reference and final artifact. All record comparisons are based on literature and registry references available as of September 16, 2026.

The current collection contains **120 record-setting results: 20 numerical bound records across 12 families** and **100 construction records across eight families**. A separate Tuza theorem extension brings the report to 21 families in total and is excluded from the record count.

We count one final result per distinct instance or parameter setting. An enclosing interval counts once, and intermediate improvements do not add records. Figure 2 gives the family breakdown.

The results repository retains the final artifacts and comparison values (Epi Team, 2026). Some evolving registries already list the new results. Our tables retain the earlier values used for comparison so the improvement remains traceable after those updates.

## 4.2 Construction Records

Of the 100 construction records, 97 concern geometric packing. The remaining three improve vehicle routing, the signed-maximum variant of the third autocorrelation inequality and a Zhang–Zagier construction. Figure 2 gives the counts for all eight families. Packing references come from Packomania and Erich Friedman’s Packing Center (Specht, 2026; Friedman, 2026). Appendix B defines the objectives and gives these three comparisons.

## 5 Case Studies

### 5.1 Refining a Published Packing

The task is to place 34 non-overlapping regular pentagons of unit side length inside an equilateral triangle of minimum side length. Each pentagon has a center and orientation. The evaluator checks containment and overlap and measures the required triangle size.

Épi starts from a published arrangement with triangle side length approximately 12.9814 (Friedman, 2026). It jointly refines the pentagons’ centers and orientations, checking containment and overlap after each candidate update. The final side length is approximately 12.9756, a reduction of 0.0445%. The released coordinates specify the construction at full precision.

Figure 3 shows nine retained geometric constructions. For pentagons, the objective reduces the size of the enclosing triangle. The circle-packing tasks increase the common radius inside a fixed container (Specht, 2026). Each panel is drawn directly from the released coordinates.

### 5.2 Separating the Cohn–Elkies Bound from Packing Density

The Cohn–Elkies method bounds sphere-packing density from above by optimizing an auxiliary function. We ask whether its best possible bound can equal the actual packing density. A strict separation would establish a limitation of the method itself.

Let \(\rho_d\) be the optimal sphere-packing center density in dimension _d_, and let _C<sub>d</sub>_ be the best upper bound attainable by the Cohn–Elkies linear program in the same normalization. Then \(\rho_d\le C_d\). To prove that the method is not sharp, it is enough to find a packing upper bound _U<sub>d</sub>_ and a lower bound _L<sub>d</sub>_ on the linear program’s optimum such that

\(\rho_d\le U_d<L_d\le C_d.\) (2)

The middle inequality creates a separation between the true packing problem and the best answer available from this method.

## 5.3 Narrowing the Interval for the _n_-Queens Constant

The number _Q(n_) of placements of _n_ non-attacking queens on an \(n\times n\) board has an asymptotic form governed by a constant \(\alpha\),

\(Q(n)=\left(ne^{-\alpha+o(1)}\right)^n.\) (3)

Bounds on \(\alpha\) can be obtained from finite convex optimization problems. Nobel et al. (2023) develop a scalable Newton method for these formulations and report the interval

\[1.944000752,1.944001082\].

Épi refines the lower and upper bounds separately. Rational feasibility checks and directed rounding give

\(1.9440010223327\le\alpha\le 1.9440010262694.\) (4)

The interval width decreases from \(3.30\times 10^{-7}\) to approximately \(3.94\times 10^{-9}\), a factor of approximately 84. Figure 5 places the two intervals on a common axis.

## 5.4 Optimizing a tion: MAX-4-CUT

Épi starts from the MAX-4-CUT gadget framework of Nagda et al. (2025) and optimizes its edge weights. With the gadget structure and relevant completeness assignments fixed, the competing colorings have objectives that are linear in those weights.

This allows the agent to normalize one side of the hardness ratio and optimize the other through a linear program. Coloring constraints enforce the required properties of the gadget.

The reference ratio follows from the gadget parameters in Lemma C.2 and the reduction in Theorem C.2 of Nagda et al. (2025). The final integer weighted gadget changes it from

\(\frac{195581}{198140}\approx 0.987085\text{to}\frac{84931}{86101}\approx 0.986411.\) (5)

The released weighted edge list and finite checks recover this ratio exactly. Substituting the new gadget into the published reduction gives the improved hardness bound. This formulation provides a reusable optimization procedure: researchers can fix the gadget structure, optimize its weights subject to explicit coloring constraints, and verify the resulting ratio exactly.

## 5.5 A Finite Construction for the Spencer Constant

The square-matrix discrepancy problem asks how well signs can balance the rows of a real matrix with entries in [-1,1]. Épi found an \(8\times 8\) matrix whose discrepancy is exactly five. Exhausting its 256 sign assignments gives row-maximum norms of five or seven, so the minimum is five. The matrix therefore raises the record lower bound on the universal constant from \(7/\sqrt{17}\) to \(5/\sqrt{8}\) (Tao et al., 2026).

Figure 5 shows the entire matrix. Its entries lie in {-1,0,1}, within the allowed range [-1,1], and the claim can be checked by enumerating its sign assignments.

## 5.6 Certifying Near-Optimal Water-Network Design

The waterund36 instance in MINLPLib minimizes the cost of a water-using network under nonlinear flow and concentration constraints (MINLPLib, 2026). A feasible network costing approximately 662.807 was already known, but the listed global lower bound was only about 655.544.

Épi tightens the lower bound to within approximately 10<sup>-5</sup> of that same feasible value, closing more than 99.999% of the MINLPLib gap. This certifies the near-optimality of the existing network. The full-precision comparison appears in Appendix A.12.

To establish the bound, the agent constructs a relaxation containing every feasible network. Exact rational inequalities then rule out objective values below the stated cutoff. The certificate therefore applies to the original nonlinear problem. Appendix A.12 explains this argument and relates the instance to earlier optimization work.

## 5.7 From Numerical Optimization to Proof: Tuza’s Conjecture

For a finite simple graph _G_, let \(\upsilon_\triangle(G)\) be the maximum number of pairwise edge-disjoint triangles and \(\tau_\triangle(G)\) the minimum size of a _triangle cover_: a set of edges meeting every triangle in _G_. Equivalently, deleting a triangle cover makes the entire graph triangle-free. Tuza’s conjecture, proposed in 1981 (Bonamy et al., 2022), asserts

\(\tau_\triangle(G)\le 2\upsilon_\triangle(G).\) (6)

Thus, if _G_ contains no _k_+1 pairwise edge-disjoint triangles, deleting at most 2_k_ edges suffices to eliminate every triangle in _G_.

**Packing and covering.** König’s theorem equates the maximum matching size and minimum vertex-cover size in a bipartite graph (König, 1931). Tuza’s conjecture concerns a matching-cover relation in the _triangle hypergraph_, whose vertices are the edges of _G_ and whose hyperedges are its triangles. Taking all edges of a maximum triangle packing gives the elementary bound \(\tau_\triangle\le 3\upsilon_\triangle\): any uncovered triangle could be added to the packing. The conjectured factor of two is attained by _K_<sub>4</sub>, where \(\upsilon_\triangle=1\) and \(\tau_\triangle=2\).

### Split graphs and prior results.

A split graph has a partition \(V(G)=C\sqcup I\), where _C_ induces a clique and _I_ is independent. Known cases include threshold graphs, whose independent-side neighborhoods are nested by inclusion (Bonamy et al., 2022), and _K_<sub>8</sub>-free chordal graphs, which include _K_<sub>8</sub>-free split graphs (Botler et al., 2021). Our eight-vertex clique part puts the family beyond the latter theorem’s _K_<sub>8</sub>-free hypothesis.

### Neighborhood types and the extension.

For \(x\in I\), let \(S_x=N_G(x)\cap C\). Since _C_ is a clique, every pair \(u,v\in S_x\) forms a triangle _xuv_. Thus _x_ is _triangle-active_ exactly when \(|S_x|\ge 2\); vertices with identical _S<sub>x</sub>_ share one _neighborhood type_. Zeng (2026) proved the conjecture for |_C_|=8 and at most two types. Épi extends this to three types with unrestricted overlaps. Their triangles can compete for the same clique edges, requiring joint covers and packings.

**Theorem 1** (Three neighborhood types)**.** _Let G be a finite simple graph with a specified partition_ \(V(G)=C\sqcup I\)_, where G[C_]=_K_<sub>8</sub> _and I is independent. Suppose that the sets_ \(N_G(x)\cap C\)_, over vertices_ \(x\in I\) _with at least two neighbors in C, take at most three distinct values. Then_ \(\tau_\triangle(G)\le 2v_\triangle(G)\).

Up to clique relabeling and type permutation, there are 872 three-type profiles: 35 have nested neighborhoods and 277 further profiles satisfy Zeng’s maximum-cut criterion. Épi constructs exact cover and packing certificates for the remaining 560 profiles, using 18,444 multiplicity boxes. An independent checker verifies the witnesses and complete profile enumeration. Zeng’s truncation lemma extends the checks to arbitrary multiplicities, establishing the result for an infinite graph family (Appendix A.13).

The proof separates the finite certificate checks from the argument extending them to arbitrary multiplicities, making explicit how the computational evidence establishes the infinite-family statement.

## 6 Épi-turbo: Fast, Low-cost Algorithm Design

### 6.1 Purpose and Design

Algorithmic coding extends Épi’s research process to the development of executable solvers. Given a problem specification and a fixed evaluator, the agent designs, implements and tests an algorithm whose solution quality and runtime are measured on new instances. Épi-turbo is a lightweight configuration for these tasks, designed to develop effective algorithms within a short campaign and a small model budget.

### Shared foundation.

Épi-turbo keeps the parts of Épi that make a result reliable. The verifier checks each candidate under a fixed ruler, and Épi keeps the research state across sessions. Branches keep each method with its code and evidence, so the agent can return to an earlier version. Memory records keep lessons and dead ends for later sessions. Épi-turbo changes how the agent uses its model budget and when the campaign stops.

### Instructions for algorithm tasks.

The task instructions tell the agent how the benchmark measures a program. They give the complete score formula, which includes the quality term and the runtime term. They also tell the agent that the final score comes from instances that the agent does not see. When a program uses a large part of its time limit, Épi-turbo tells the agent. Thus the agent can find a good balance between solution quality and runtime. The instructions do not contain methods or hints for a specific problem.

### Model calls for algorithm design.

Each model call has a cost, and a short task has a small number of calls. Épi-turbo tells the agent that every call costs money, which includes a check on an active job. The agent does short experiments with a time limit in its own session. It sends an experiment to the execution infrastructure only when the experiment needs more time than a session gives. It examines active jobs only when a result can change its next decision. As a result, most of the budget goes to the design and test of algorithms.

### Continuous sessions.

Épi-turbo runs each campaign as one continuous session if possible. The session continues the best method so far and does not restart from an empty context. Before a session ends, the agent records its state, its best candidate and its next steps. The next session reads this record and continues the<tbc>

work. Épi-turbo stops the campaign when more sessions do not improve the best verified score. Thus the agent does not use more budget on a task where it finds no improvement.

**Budget control.** Épi-turbo reserves the maximum cost of a model call before the call starts. It also keeps a small part of the budget for the end of the campaign. Thus the cost of a campaign is never more than its budget, and the final steps always have funds. The reservation uses the price limits of the model, so the agent can use almost all of its budget.

**Optional components.** Independent review and extra validation are optional in Épi-turbo. On short tasks, their cost was larger than their benefit in our tests. Both components were off in the runs below.

## 6.2 Benchmark and Protocol

We use FrontierOR, a benchmark of 180 operations-research tasks from the literature (Kong et al., 2026). Each task asks for a standalone program that solves new instances of one problem class. The program must not call an external optimization solver. The baseline is x (OpenAI, 2026), a widely used coding agent, with GPT-6-Astra as its model. Épi-turbo uses the same model with the same reasoning effort.

We selected 30 tasks that were new to both systems. We took them in the official hardness order of the benchmark and excluded tasks with unreliable reference values. Of these tasks, 13 are in the hard split, and 17 have hardness ranks 51 to 70. For each task, each system had a model budget of $20. We did one run for each task and system, so we do not report statistical significance.

The evaluator first runs each program on two development instances. The agent sees these results during the campaign. After the campaign, the best development program runs once on four held-out instances. Each held-out run has a time limit of one hour. The benchmark score has a quality term and a speed term.

The quality term decreases as the gap to the reference value increases. The speed term compares the runtime of the program with the runtime of the reference solver. It counts only when the solution is within 1% of the reference value. Outside this 1% band, the score is the quality term alone. The reference values come from a commercial solver, and some of them are weak. Thus we also compare the two systems on each instance directly, with their objective values only.

## 8 Autonomous Research for Human Understanding

Our goal with Épi is to make autonomous research contribute to human understanding: researchers should be able to explain why a result holds, identify what it reveals about the problem, and use that knowledge to guide further work. Achieving this goal requires connecting computational artifacts to explicit formulations, mathematical arguments, and the scientific questions they resolve. Épi builds on existing theory and retains the implementations, experiments, and assessments through which its methods develop. The case studies illustrate how this process can produce knowledge that researchers can use: the Cohn–Elkies separation identifies a structural limit of an established method; the MAX-4-CUT formulation provides a reusable procedure for optimizing gadget weights; and the Tuza proof makes explicit how finite certificates establish a statement about an infinite graph family. These examples express our broader aim for self-improvement: an agent should accumulate both the ability to obtain better results and knowledge that helps people understand and extend those results.

## 9 Conclusion

Épi is an autonomous research agent that sustains investigations across model sessions and improves its methods through memory, branching and independent review. Its campaigns produced 120 record-setting results and a computer-assisted proof of a new case of Tuza’s conjecture. The released constructions and certificates provide concrete, checkable evidence for these advances. Épi-turbo extends this research process to algorithmic coding across routing, scheduling, planning and graph optimization. On 30 FrontierOR tasks, it achieves a 5.4% higher total benchmark score than x with the same model while using 64% of its model cost.

Épi couples method improvement with a persistent record of implementations, experiments, and review. This record supports inspection of the research process, while explicit constructions and proof arguments make the resulting findings available for further scientific work. Together, these evaluations demonstrate the applicability of persistent, feedback-driven method development to mathematical discovery and efficient algorithm design.

## A.13 Tuza’s Conjecture: Proof for Three Neighborhood Types

For the partition in Theorem 1, discard independent vertices with fewer than two clique neighbors: they occur in no triangle. The remaining vertices have at most three distinct neighborhoods in _C_. We call a triple of these neighborhoods, considered up to relabeling _C_ and permuting the three types, a neighborhood profile.

### Finite reduction.

Zeng’s multiplicity-truncation lemma (Zeng, 2026) preserves both \(\tau_\Delta\) and \(\upsilon_\Delta\) when each type is truncated to 28 copies. Every triangle uses a clique edge, so a packing uses at most 28 triangles and at most 28 independent vertices of any type. For covers, all 28 clique edges suffice. If a minimum cover of the truncated graph has fewer than 28 edges, some copy of every saturated type has no incident cover edge. All clique edges within that type’s neighborhood must then be covered, which also covers triangles through any additional copies. Thus the finite multiplicity range suffices for the infinite statement.

### Completeness and certificates.

An independent enumeration gives 872 profiles with three distinct active types. Of these, 35 have nested neighborhoods and fall under the threshold-graph theorem of Bonamy et al. (2022). Another 277 satisfy Zeng’s maximum-cut criterion (Zeng, 2026). The cases with at most two types follow from Zeng’s theorem. The remaining 560 profiles are covered by exact certificates containing 18,444 integer boxes in {0_,...,_28}<sup>3</sup>.

For a box with componentwise bounds \(\ell\le m\le u\), the certificate gives a triangle cover _Fu_ meeting every triangle in the upper-multiplicity graph _Gu_ and an edge-disjoint triangle packing \(P_\ell\) in the lower-multiplicity graph \(G_\ell\), satisfying \(|F_u|\le 2|P_\ell|\). The cover meets both the triangles inside _C_ and every triangle _xuv_ with \(x\in I\) and \(u,v\in N_G(x)\cap C\). Adding copies preserves the smaller graph as a subgraph. Hence

\(\tau_\triangle(G_m)\le|F_u|\le 2|P_\ell|\le 2\nu_\triangle(G_m).\)

A separate checker reconstructs the graphs, enumerates every triangle in each upper-multiplicity graph, checks that its stored cover meets every such triangle, and verifies that the stored packing consists of edge- disjoint triangles in the lower-multiplicity graph. It also checks the cardinality inequality and coverage of every integer multiplicity vector. All 560 profiles and 18,444 boxes passed. The certificates cover the remaining profiles, and truncation extends the conclusion to arbitrary multiplicities. This proves Theorem 1.
